questions.questionText: Four CDMA stations use the Walsh codes A = [+1, +1, +1, +1], B = [+1, −1, +1, −1], C = [+1, +1, −1, −1] and D = [+1, −1, −1, +1]. A sends 1, B sends 0, C is silent and D sends 1 (bit 1 = +code, bit 0 = −code, silent = 0). A receiver decodes the channel signal with C's code. What does it obtain?
options: A value that depends on the other stations' data
questions.explanation: The channel carries A − B + D = [+1, +1, −1, +3]. Its inner product with C is 1 + 1 + 1 − 3 = 0, and 0 / 4 = 0, so C sent nothing; because the codes are orthogonal, the other stations' data cancel out completely.

subtopics.title: LAN Standards: Ethernet, Token Bus, Token Ring & Wireless LANs
subtopics.subtitle: IEEE 802.3 frame, Ethernet media names, 802.4, 802.5, 802.11 WLAN and Bluetooth

concepts.text: The IEEE 802 Family
Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)

Ethernet is the dominant wired LAN. Classic Ethernet was a shared bus using 1-persistent CSMA/CD and Manchester encoding at 10 Mbps; modern Ethernet uses switches and full-duplex links, so collisions no longer occur, but the frame format is unchanged. Every frame carries 48-bit source and destination MAC addresses and a CRC-32 trailer.

rows: 10101011, marks the start of the frame
EtherType (e.g. 0x0800 IPv4) or length of data (≤ 1500)
Payload, padded up to 46 bytes if shorter
CRC-32 over addresses, type and data

concepts.text: Frame size is counted from the destination address to the CRC: minimum 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes and maximum 6 + 6 + 2 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes. The 64-byte minimum comes from the CSMA/CD round-trip rule; the preamble and SFD are not counted. After each frame there is an inter-frame gap of 96 bit times.
Reading Ethernet media names (speed + BASE for baseband + medium):
items: 10BASE5 (thick coax, 500 m) and 10BASE2 (thin coax, about 185 m): 10 Mbps bus.
10BASE-T: 10 Mbps over twisted pair (Cat 3) to a hub/switch, 100 m.
100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet): 100 Mbps over two pairs of Cat 5 UTP; 100BASE-FX over fibre.
1000BASE-T (Gigabit): 1 Gbps over four pairs of Cat 5e; 1000BASE-SX/LX over multimode/single-mode fibre.
10GBASE-T and faster use full duplex only, so CSMA/CD is not used.

concepts.text: Token Bus (802.4) and Token Ring (802.5)

Token bus arranges stations on a physical bus (usually broadband coaxial cable) but passes a token in a logical ring by descending address. Only the token holder may transmit, so the maximum waiting time is bounded, which suited factory automation (the MAP protocol). Token ring connects stations in a physical ring (star-wired through MAUs in practice) at 4 or 16 Mbps using differential Manchester coding. A 3-byte token (start delimiter, access control, end delimiter) circulates; a station seizes it, sends its frame, and the frame returns to the sender, which removes it and releases the token. The access control byte has 3 priority bits and 3 reservation bits, and an active monitor station regenerates lost tokens and removes orphan frames.
Wireless LANs (IEEE 802.11)

An 802.11 Basic Service Set (BSS) is a group of stations; an ad hoc (independent) BSS has no access point, while an infrastructure BSS has an access point (AP) connecting it to a wired distribution system. Several BSSs joined by a distribution system form an Extended Service Set (ESS), which lets users roam between APs. Access uses CSMA/CA (DCF) with optional RTS/CTS, and every unicast frame is acknowledged.
Problems specific to wireless LANs:
items: Hidden terminal: A and C both reach B but not each other, so carrier sensing fails and their frames collide at B. RTS/CTS solves it because C hears B's CTS and defers.
Exposed terminal: B refrains from sending to A because it hears C sending to D, although the two transmissions would not interfere.
Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1): short-range 2.4 GHz personal area network; a master and up to 7 active slaves form a piconet, using frequency hopping.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Ethernet, Token LANs and Wi-Fi

Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) is the most common wired LAN: every frame carries MAC addresses, speeds have grown from 10 Mbps through 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps and beyond, and CSMA/CD is used on the old shared, half-duplex segments. In token ring (IEEE 802.5) the stations form a ring and a token travels round it; only the token holder may transmit, so there are no collisions at all (not merely fewer), but in a simple ring one broken link or station stops the whole network, which is why real rings were star-wired through MAUs that bypass a failed station. Token bus (IEEE 802.4) combines the two ideas: the cabling is a bus like Ethernet, but access follows a token passed round a logical ring in descending order of station address, so the waiting time is bounded. Each token bus station knows its successor, and new stations join through periodic solicit-successor frames sent by the token holder.

rows: Thick / thin coaxial bus, 500 m / 185 m
2 pairs of Cat 3 UTP to a hub or switch, 100 m
Multimode fibre, 2 km in full duplex
4 pairs of Cat 5e UTP, 100 m, 250 Mbps per pair
Multimode fibre up to 550 m / single-mode fibre 5 km
Multimode 300 m / single-mode 10 km / Cat 6a 100 m; full duplex only

concepts.text: Manchester coding puts a transition in the middle of every bit, so the receiver recovers the clock from the signal itself and the line carries no DC component. The price is bandwidth: every bit needs two signal elements, so 10 Mbps Ethernet signals at 20 Mbaud. Fast Ethernet therefore switched to 4B/5B block coding, which sends every 4 data bits as a 5-bit code word chosen so that no more than three 0s ever occur in a row, an overhead of 25 % instead of 100 %. Differential Manchester, used by 802.5 token ring, also has a mid-bit transition in every bit but encodes a 0 as a transition at the start of the bit and a 1 as no transition there, so it does not depend on the polarity of the wires.

Worked trace: Manchester, IEEE 802.3 convention (1 = low->high, 0 = high->low)
Bits:         1     0     1     1     0
Half-bits:   L H   H L   L H   L H   H L
Mid-bit transitions: 5, one in every bit (this is the clock)
Bit-boundary transitions: only between two equal bits (the 1-1 pair here): 1
Total = 6 transitions; 10 signal elements for 5 bits, so baud = 2 x bit rate
The opposite polarity convention (used in some textbooks) gives the same counts

concepts.plainText: Wire time of one Ethernet frame T_wire = 8 × (L + 20) / R, where L is the frame size in bytes from destination address to FCS (64 to 1518) and 20 bytes = 8 preamble/SFD + 12 inter-frame gap; payload efficiency η = P / (P + 38) for a payload of P = 46 to 1500 bytes (38 = 8 + 14 header + 4 FCS + 12 gap).

concepts.text:
Worked example: Ethernet overhead and frame rate at 1 Gbps (1 Gbps = 10^9 bit/s)
Per frame on the wire: preamble + SFD 8 + header 14 + data + FCS 4 + inter-frame gap 12 bytes
Minimum frame: 8 + 64 + 12 = 84 bytes = 672 bits -> 672 ns
  frame rate = 10^9 / 672 = 1 488 095 frames/s; payload efficiency = 46 / 84 = 54.8 %
Maximum frame: 8 + 1518 + 12 = 1538 bytes = 12 304 bits -> 12.304 us
  frame rate = 10^9 / 12 304 = 81 274 frames/s; payload efficiency = 1500 / 1538 = 97.5 %
Useful IP data rate with full frames = 0.975 x 1000 Mbps = 975 Mbps

In 802.5 a free token is 3 bytes (start delimiter, access control, end delimiter); a station that wants to send flips the token bit in the access control byte, turning the token into the start of a data frame, and may keep it for the token holding time, 10 ms by default. The frame travels all the way round and the sender removes it (source stripping), reading the A and C bits of the frame status byte to learn whether the destination recognised its address and copied the frame. With early token release, used on 16 Mbps rings, the sender issues a new token straight after its frame instead of waiting for the frame to return. Ring latency is the propagation time round the ring plus about one bit of delay in each station, and the active monitor adds a 24-bit latency buffer so that a whole token always fits on a short ring.

rows: 0 / 0: station to station in one BSS

concepts.text:
Worked trace: A sends to B; C is hidden from A but in range of B (802.11 DCF with RTS/CTS)
Medium idle for DIFS and A's backoff reaches 0
A -> B  RTS  Duration = 3 SIFS + CTS + DATA + ACK     C cannot hear it
        SIFS
B -> A  CTS  Duration = 2 SIFS + DATA + ACK           C hears it, sets NAV and stays silent
        SIFS
A -> B  DATA                                         stations near A deferred on the RTS
        SIFS
B -> A  ACK                                          NAVs expire; contention restarts after DIFS
More on 802.11 and Bluetooth:
items: DCF (distributed coordination function) is the mandatory CSMA/CA mode; PCF (point coordination function) is an optional contention-free mode in which the AP polls stations, taking priority by waiting only PIFS; a beacon opens each contention-free period, which is followed by an ordinary contention period.
Exposed station problem: B hears C sending to D and defers, although its own frame to A would not disturb D's reception; RTS/CTS does not cure it, because B still hears C's traffic.
802.11 frame types: management (beacon, probe, authentication, association), control (RTS, CTS, ACK) and data.

Speeds such as 300+ Mbps for 802.11n and 1+ Gbps for 802.11ac are typical figures for two or three spatial streams; the standards' maxima are 600 Mbps and about 6.9 Gbps. 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) adds 320 MHz channels and multi-link operation.

Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) uses the 2.4 GHz band with frequency hopping over 79 channels of 1 MHz at 1600 hops/s; a piconet has one master (central) and up to 7 active slaves plus up to 255 parked ones, and piconets linked through a shared device form a scatternet. Bluetooth Low Energy uses 40 channels of 2 MHz.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: including the 8-byte preamble and SFD in the 64 to 1518-byte frame size, yet forgetting them and the 12-byte inter-frame gap when working out wire time or frame rate; confusing Manchester's baud rate (twice the bit rate) with its bit rate; saying token ring has fewer collisions (it has none); and mixing up 802.4 (token bus: physical bus, logical ring) with 802.5 (token ring: physical ring).

10 Mbps Ethernet slot time = 512 bits / 10 Mbps = 51.2 us

notes.text: Map numbers to names: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.4 token bus, 802.5 token ring, 802.11 Wi-Fi, 802.15 Bluetooth. Ethernet data field 46–1500 bytes, frame 64–1518 bytes.
Do not include the 8-byte preamble and SFD when stating Ethernet minimum or maximum frame size; they belong to the physical layer.
The 1500-byte Ethernet payload limit is the MTU seen by IP; larger IP datagrams must be fragmented or the path MTU reduced.

flashcards.front: What does 100BASE-TX mean?
flashcards.back: 100 Mbps, baseband signalling, over twisted-pair copper (two pairs of Cat 5 UTP): Fast Ethernet.

flashcards.front: What is the role of the active monitor in 802.5 token ring?
flashcards.back: It supervises the ring: regenerates a lost token, removes frames that circulate endlessly and provides the master clock.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a BSS and an ESS in 802.11?
flashcards.back: A BSS is one cell of stations (with or without an AP); an ESS is several infrastructure BSSs joined by a distribution system so users can roam.

flashcards.front: How does token bus differ from token ring physically?
flashcards.back: Token bus uses a physical bus with a logical ring for token passing; token ring uses an actual physical ring of point-to-point links.

questions.questionText: What is the minimum size of the data (payload) field in an IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frame?
questions.explanation: The data field is 46–1500 bytes; 46 bytes plus 18 bytes of header and CRC give the 64-byte minimum frame.

questions.questionText: Which IEEE standard defines the token bus LAN?
questions.explanation: 802.4 is token bus; 802.3 is Ethernet, 802.5 token ring and 802.11 wireless LAN.

questions.questionText: In an 802.11 WLAN, which mechanism addresses the hidden terminal problem?
questions.explanation: A station hidden from the sender still hears the receiver's CTS and defers, preventing a collision at the receiver.

questions.questionText: Which Wi-Fi standard operates only in the 5 GHz band and supports multi-gigabit rates with MU-MIMO?
questions.explanation: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) is 5 GHz only with rates up to about 6.9 Gbps; b and g are 2.4 GHz, n is dual-band.

questions.questionText: Which LAN technology does the IEEE 802.3 standard define?
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.3 is Ethernet. Token ring is 802.5, Wi-Fi is 802.11 and Bluetooth is 802.15.1.

questions.questionText: Which LAN standard connects the stations in a physical ring and lets only the station holding the circulating token transmit?
questions.explanation: Token ring (802.5) passes the token round a physical ring (star-wired through MAUs in practice). Token bus (802.4) also uses a token, but over a physical bus with a logical ring, and Ethernet uses CSMA/CD.

questions.questionText: An Ethernet receiver silently discards a frame whose CRC check fails and sends no acknowledgement. In the TCP/IP stack, which protocol makes sure the lost data is still delivered to the application?
questions.explanation: Ethernet gives an unacknowledged connectionless service, UDP never retransmits and CSMA/CD only resolves collisions. TCP numbers and acknowledges its segments, so a segment lost in a discarded frame is retransmitted end to end.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum data rate of IEEE 802.11b?
questions.explanation: 802.11b (2.4 GHz, DSSS/CCK) tops out at 11 Mbps. The original 802.11 gave 2 Mbps, 802.11a/g 54 Mbps and 802.11n up to 600 Mbps.

questions.questionText: 10 Mbps Ethernet uses Manchester encoding. What signal-element (baud) rate does this need on the cable?
questions.explanation: Each Manchester bit is sent as two half-bit signal elements, so the baud rate is 2 × 10 Mbps = 20 Mbaud. This 100 % overhead is why faster Ethernets moved to block codes such as 4B/5B.

questions.questionText: The bits 0 1 1 1 1 are sent with Manchester encoding (IEEE 802.3 convention: 0 = high-to-low, 1 = low-to-high). How many signal-level transitions occur within these five bit periods, counting mid-bit and bit-boundary transitions but not any transition before the first bit?
questions.explanation: Every bit has one mid-bit transition (5), and a boundary transition is needed only between two equal bits, because the first bit then ends on the opposite level to the one the second must start on; 0 1 1 1 1 has three such 1-1 boundaries, giving 5 + 3 = 8. The count is the same under either polarity convention.

questions.questionText: In the name 10BASE-T, what do the three parts mean?
options: 10 Mbps, broadband signalling, thick coaxial cable
10 km maximum length, baseband signalling, twisted pair
10 stations per segment, baseband signalling, terminated bus
questions.explanation: The number is the data rate in Mbps, BASE means baseband (one signal occupies the medium) and T means twisted pair. 10BASE5 and 10BASE2 were the coaxial versions.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum segment length of 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX and 1000BASE-T twisted-pair Ethernet?
questions.explanation: All twisted-pair Ethernet standards up to 1000BASE-T (and 10GBASE-T on Cat 6a) allow 100 m per segment. 185 m and 500 m are the 10BASE2 and 10BASE5 coax limits, and 2 km is 100BASE-FX over multimode fibre.

questions.questionText: 100BASE-TX applies 4B/5B block coding before MLT-3 line coding. What is the resulting signalling rate on the wire (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s)?
questions.explanation: 4B/5B turns every 4 data bits into 5 code bits, so 100 Mbps × 5/4 = 125 Mbit/s of code bits, sent by MLT-3 at 125 Mbaud. 100 Mbaud ignores the block code and 200 Mbaud would be Manchester.

questions.questionText: How does 1000BASE-T carry 1 Gbps over Category 5e cable?
options: It uses one pair at 1 Gbps with Manchester coding
It uses two pairs, one for each direction, at 500 Mbps each
It uses 8B/10B coding on a single pair at 1.25 Gbaud
It uses all four pairs at once, 250 Mbps per pair in both directions, with PAM-5 signalling
questions.explanation: 1000BASE-T sends 250 Mbps on each of the four pairs simultaneously in both directions (echo cancellation separates them), using PAM-5 at 125 Mbaud per pair. 8B/10B at 1.25 Gbaud is used by the fibre versions 1000BASE-SX/LX.

questions.questionText: Which statement about 10 Gigabit Ethernet (IEEE 802.3ae / 802.3an) is correct?
options: It keeps CSMA/CD but with a 4096-bit slot time
It operates in full-duplex mode only, so CSMA/CD is not used
It works only over coaxial cable
It uses a different frame format with 128-bit addresses
questions.explanation: 10 Gigabit Ethernet supports only full-duplex point-to-point links, so there is no contention and no CSMA/CD, while the 802.3 frame format and 48-bit MAC addresses stay the same. The 4096-bit slot belonged to half-duplex Gigabit Ethernet.

questions.questionText: A 200-byte IP packet is sent in an Ethernet II frame. Counting the preamble and SFD (8 bytes), the MAC header (14 bytes), the FCS (4 bytes) and the 12-byte inter-frame gap, what fraction of the wire time carries the IP packet?
questions.explanation: Wire bytes = 8 + 14 + 200 + 4 + 12 = 238, so the fraction is 200 / 238 = 84.0%. Leaving out the gap gives 200 / 226 = 88.5%, and counting only header and FCS gives 200 / 218 = 91.7%.

questions.questionText: 10 Mbps Ethernet (10^7 bit/s) sends back-to-back minimum-size frames. Including the 8-byte preamble/SFD and the 12-byte inter-frame gap, what is the maximum frame rate?
questions.explanation: Each minimum frame occupies 8 + 64 + 12 = 84 bytes = 672 bit times, so the rate is 10^7 / 672 ≈ 14,881 frames/s. Ignoring the gap gives 10^7 / 576 ≈ 17,361, ignoring preamble and gap gives 19,531, and 813 frames/s is the rate for maximum-size frames.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 packet of 30 bytes is carried in an Ethernet II frame. How many pad bytes must be added?
questions.explanation: The data field must be at least 46 bytes, so 46 − 30 = 16 pad bytes are added, making the frame 14 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes. 34 wrongly pads up to 64 bytes of data.

questions.questionText: The Type/Length field of a received Ethernet frame contains 0x05DC (1500 decimal). How is it interpreted?
options: As the length of the data field, because values up to 1500 denote a length
As an error, because the field must always be at least 0x0600
questions.explanation: Values up to 1500 (0x05DC) are IEEE 802.3 length fields, and values of 1536 (0x0600) or more are EtherTypes such as 0x0800 for IPv4 or 0x8100 for a VLAN tag. So 0x05DC means a 1500-byte data field, normally beginning with an LLC header.

questions.questionText: How does classic Bluetooth share the crowded 2.4 GHz band with Wi-Fi and other devices?
options: CSMA/CD on a single 20 MHz channel
Token passing among all nearby devices
Fixed-frequency transmission in the 5 GHz band
Frequency hopping over 79 channels of 1 MHz, about 1600 hops per second
questions.explanation: Classic Bluetooth (802.15.1) uses frequency-hopping spread spectrum: the piconet hops over 79 one-megahertz channels about 1600 times per second, so interference on any one frequency affects only a few slots. Bluetooth Low Energy uses 40 channels of 2 MHz.

questions.questionText: In IEEE 802.5 token ring, which station removes a data frame from the ring?
options: The sending station, when the frame returns to it
The destination station, as soon as it copies the frame
The active monitor, in every case
The next station downstream of the destination
questions.explanation: Token ring uses source stripping: the frame circles the ring and the sender removes it, reading the A and C bits to see whether the destination recognised and copied it. The active monitor removes only orphan frames whose sender has failed.

questions.questionText: What does a free token consist of in IEEE 802.5 token ring?
options: 1 byte: the access control byte only
6 bytes: the address of the next station
3 bytes: start delimiter, access control and end delimiter
questions.explanation: The 802.5 token is 3 bytes: SD, AC and ED. A station seizes it by flipping the token bit in the AC byte, which turns it into the start of a data frame.

questions.questionText: Which of these is a job of the active monitor in an IEEE 802.5 token ring?
options: Assigning IP addresses to the ring stations
Detecting collisions and sending jam signals
Converting token ring frames into Ethernet frames
Regenerating a lost token and removing frames that would otherwise circle the ring endlessly
questions.explanation: One station acts as active monitor: it supplies the master clock, regenerates the token if none is seen in time, uses the monitor bit to remove orphan frames and inserts a latency buffer. Token rings have no collisions, so there is no jam signal.

questions.questionText: In IEEE 802.4 token bus, in what order is the token passed?
options: Round a logical ring in descending order of station address
In order of the stations' physical position along the cable
To whichever station has the most data waiting
In a random order chosen by a central controller
questions.explanation: Token bus stations sit on a physical bus but form a logical ring ordered by address, with the token passed from higher to lower address and each station knowing its successor. Physical position on the cable does not matter.

questions.questionText: A 16 Mbps token ring is 2 km long (signal speed 2 × 10^8 m/s) and has 50 stations, each adding a 1-bit delay. What is the ring latency in bits?
questions.explanation: Propagation round the ring = 2000 / (2 × 10^8) = 10 µs, which is 10 µs × 16 × 10^6 bit/s = 160 bits; adding 50 × 1 bit of station delay gives 210 bits. 370 bits wrongly doubles the propagation delay, as if it were a round trip.

questions.questionText: Several 802.11 BSSs whose access points are joined by a distribution system, so that users can roam between them, form a(n):
questions.explanation: An ESS is two or more infrastructure BSSs connected through a distribution system (usually wired Ethernet) and sharing one SSID. An IBSS is an ad hoc network without an AP, and piconets and scatternets are Bluetooth terms.

questions.questionText: Which 802.11 access mode is optional and contention-free, with the access point polling the stations?
questions.explanation: In the point coordination function the AP (point coordinator) polls stations during a contention-free period, gaining priority by waiting only PIFS. DCF is the mandatory contention-based CSMA/CA mode, and EDCA is the prioritised contention mode of 802.11e.

questions.questionText: Station B wants to send to A but hears C transmitting to D. B defers, even though its transmission to A would not interfere with D's reception. What is this called?
questions.explanation: B is exposed to C's transmission and needlessly stays silent, wasting capacity. In the hidden station problem the opposite happens: two senders cannot hear each other and collide at a common receiver.

questions.questionText: Which sequence correctly shows an 802.11 DCF exchange that uses RTS/CTS?
options: SIFS, RTS, DIFS, CTS, DIFS, DATA, DIFS, ACK
DIFS, DATA, SIFS, RTS, SIFS, CTS, SIFS, ACK
DIFS, RTS, SIFS, CTS, SIFS, DATA, SIFS, ACK
questions.explanation: The sender waits DIFS (plus any backoff) before the RTS; every later frame of the exchange (CTS, DATA and ACK) follows after only SIFS, so no other station can slip in. Using DIFS inside the exchange would let contending stations interrupt it.

questions.questionText: Which IEEE 802.11 amendment is marketed as Wi-Fi 6 and introduced OFDMA?
questions.explanation: 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6 (Wi-Fi 6E when extended to 6 GHz) and adds OFDMA and 1024-QAM. 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4 and 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing 802.11a and 802.11g is correct?
options: Both reach 54 Mbps using OFDM, but 802.11a works at 5 GHz and 802.11g at 2.4 GHz
802.11a reaches 11 Mbps and 802.11g 54 Mbps, both at 2.4 GHz
Both work at 5 GHz, but only 802.11g uses OFDM
802.11g is backward compatible with 802.11a but not with 802.11b
questions.explanation: 802.11a and 802.11g share the same OFDM physical layer and 54 Mbps maximum, but 802.11a uses 5 GHz while 802.11g uses 2.4 GHz and stays backward compatible with 802.11b.

questions.questionText: How many active slave devices can a single Bluetooth piconet master serve at once?
questions.explanation: A piconet has one master (central) and at most 7 active slaves, because the active member address is 3 bits and one value is reserved. Up to 255 further devices can be parked, and 8 counts the master as well.

questions.questionText: A wireless station sends a frame through its access point to a host on the wired LAN, so To DS = 1 and From DS = 0. What does Address 1 of the 802.11 frame contain?
questions.explanation: Address 1 is always the immediate receiver, here the AP, identified by the BSSID. Address 2 holds the sending station and Address 3 the final destination, the wired host.

questions.questionText: A 100 Mbps Ethernet link carries back-to-back maximum-size frames, each holding a 1500-byte IP packet with 20-byte IP and 20-byte TCP headers and no options. Counting preamble and SFD (8 bytes), MAC header and FCS (18 bytes) and the 12-byte inter-frame gap, what is the maximum TCP payload (goodput) rate?
questions.explanation: Each frame uses 8 + 18 + 1500 + 12 = 1538 bytes of wire time and carries 1500 − 40 = 1460 bytes of TCP payload, so goodput = 100 × 1460 / 1538 ≈ 94.9 Mbps. Forgetting the TCP/IP headers gives 97.5 Mbps, and forgetting preamble and gap gives 96.2 Mbps.

subtopics.title: LAN Addressing, ARP, PPP & WAN Protocols
subtopics.subtitle: MAC addresses, ARP, PPP with PAP/CHAP, and WAN protocols: HDLC, Frame Relay, ATM

concepts.text: LAN (MAC) Addressing

Every network interface has a 48-bit (6-byte) MAC address, written as 12 hexadecimal digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The first 24 bits are the Organisationally Unique Identifier (OUI) assigned by IEEE to the manufacturer, and the last 24 bits are assigned by the vendor. MAC addresses are flat (not hierarchical) and identify a node on the local link only; IP addresses handle end-to-end delivery.
Kinds of MAC destination address:
items: Unicast: least significant bit of the first byte is 0; delivered to one interface.
Multicast: least significant bit of the first byte is 1 (e.g. 01:00:5E:xx:xx:xx for IPv4 multicast); delivered to a group.
Broadcast: all 48 bits are 1, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF; received by every station on the LAN.
The second-least significant bit of the first byte distinguishes universally administered (0) from locally administered (1) addresses.

concepts.text: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)

Before a host can send an IP packet on a LAN it needs the MAC address of the next hop (the destination host or the default gateway). ARP resolves this mapping dynamically. The sender broadcasts an ARP request (destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, EtherType 0x0806) asking who owns the target IP; only the owner replies with a unicast ARP reply containing its MAC address. Both sides store the mapping in an ARP cache with a timeout (typically a few minutes), so later packets need no new request.
ARP variants and related protocols:
items: Proxy ARP: a router answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts on another network, so hosts without proper routes can still reach them.
Gratuitous ARP: a host announces its own IP-to-MAC mapping to detect duplicate IPs or update caches after failover.
RARP: the reverse, MAC to IP, used by diskless hosts at boot; replaced by BOOTP and DHCP. InARP: finds the IP address for a known Frame Relay DLCI.
Security: ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing/poisoning enables man-in-the-middle attacks; dynamic ARP inspection on switches counters it.

concepts.text: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol)

PPP is a byte-oriented data link protocol for direct links such as dial-up, DSL (PPPoE) and serial router links. Its HDLC-like frame is Flag 0x7E, Address 0xFF, Control 0x03, Protocol (2 bytes), Payload (default up to 1500 bytes) and FCS (2 or 4 bytes), with byte stuffing using escape 0x7D. PPP adds link negotiation, authentication and support for multiple network protocols, but no numbered flow control.
PPP components and phases:
items: LCP (Link Control Protocol, 0xC021): establishes, configures (MRU, authentication type, compression) and tests the link.
NCP (Network Control Protocols): one per network protocol; IPCP (0x8021) negotiates IP addresses for IPv4.
Phases: Dead, Establish (LCP), Authenticate (optional), Network (NCP), Open (data transfer), Terminate, back to Dead.
Authentication: PAP or CHAP, compared below.

rows: Two-way: user name and password sent, ACK/NAK
Never sent; response is an MD5 hash of challenge and secret
Random challenge each time, repeated periodically

concepts.text: Wide Area Protocols

X.25 is an older ITU packet-switching standard with error and flow control at every hop, suited to noisy analogue lines but slow. Frame Relay removed hop-by-hop error correction for speed; virtual circuits are identified by a 10-bit DLCI, and the Committed Information Rate (CIR) is the rate the carrier guarantees, with excess frames marked discard-eligible. ATM switches fixed 53-byte cells (5-byte header, 48-byte payload) over virtual paths and circuits (VPI/VCI), giving predictable delay for voice and video. MPLS forwards packets by short labels (a 32-bit shim header with a 20-bit label) placed between the layer 2 and layer 3 headers, often called layer 2.5, and is the basis of most modern carrier VPNs and traffic engineering.

rows: Sliding-window ARQ; basis of PPP, LAPB
Error control at every node; slow
Label switching between L2 and L3

concepts.text: Going Deeper: MAC Addressing, ARP, PPP and WAN Links

ARP exists because the two layers speak different languages: the network layer addresses packets with logical IP addresses, while the data link layer can deliver a frame only to a physical MAC address, so every link needs a translation. It works in three steps: the sender broadcasts “Who has 192.168.1.5?”, the owner of that address answers “I do, my MAC is …”, and the sender keeps the answer in its ARP cache for later packets. RARP did the reverse, MAC to IP, for diskless machines at boot, but it is obsolete and was replaced by BOOTP and then DHCP. PPP connects exactly two devices over a direct link, such as a dial-up modem connection, a DSL line (as PPPoE) or a serial link between routers, and adds authentication and error detection: a frame whose FCS fails is simply discarded, because PPP does not retransmit.

rows: The address being resolved; total 28 bytes

concepts.text:
Worked trace: A (192.168.1.10, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A) sends to B (192.168.1.5) on the same /24
1. A's ARP cache has no entry for 192.168.1.5
2. A -> all: Ethernet dst FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, type 0x0806, ARP operation 1
             'who has 192.168.1.5? tell 192.168.1.10 at 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A'
3. Every host reads it; only B answers, and B also caches A's mapping from the request
4. B -> A:   Ethernet dst 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A, type 0x0806, ARP operation 2
             '192.168.1.5 is at 00:1A:2B:00:00:05'
5. A caches 192.168.1.5 -> 00:1A:2B:00:00:05 and sends the IP packet (type 0x0800)
Off-subnet destination such as 8.8.8.8: A ARPs for its default gateway's IP instead;
the frame goes to the gateway's MAC while the IP header still says 8.8.8.8

The first byte of a MAC address carries two flag bits. Its least significant bit, the I/G bit, is 0 for an individual (unicast) address and 1 for a group (multicast) address, and it is the very first bit on an Ethernet wire because each byte is sent least significant bit first. The next bit, U/L, is 0 for a universally administered address built on an IEEE-assigned OUI and 1 for a locally administered one, such as the random addresses phones use for Wi-Fi privacy or the 02:42:… addresses Docker gives containers. IPv4 multicast groups map onto MAC addresses by placing the low 23 bits of the group address after the prefix 01:00:5E, so 2^5 = 32 groups share each multicast MAC and the receiving host must still check the destination IP address.

Worked example 1: IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.251 (mDNS) -> Ethernet MAC
224.0.0.251 = 1110 0000 . 0000 0000 . 0000 0000 . 1111 1011
Low 23 bits = 000 0000 . 0000 0000 . 1111 1011 -> 00:00:FB
MAC = 01:00:5E, then a 0 bit, then those 23 bits = 01:00:5E:00:00:FB
224.128.0.251 and 225.0.0.251 map to the same MAC (32 groups in all)
Worked example 2: MAC 02:42:AC:11:00:02
First byte 0x02 = 0000 0010 -> I/G bit 0 = unicast, U/L bit 1 = locally administered

concepts.plainText: ATM with AAL5: a packet of L bytes plus the 8-byte AAL5 trailer is padded to a multiple of 48 bytes, so it needs N = ceil((L + 8) / 48) cells of 53 bytes, and the efficiency is L / (53 × N).

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: IP packets over ATM with AAL5 (8-byte trailer, pad to a multiple of 48)
1000-byte packet: (1000 + 8) / 48 = 21 -> 21 cells, no padding needed
  bytes on the line = 21 x 53 = 1113 -> efficiency 1000 / 1113 = 89.8 %
40-byte TCP ACK:  (40 + 8) / 48 = 1 -> 1 cell of 53 bytes -> efficiency 75.5 %
41-byte packet:   (41 + 8) / 48 = 1.02 -> 2 cells = 106 bytes -> efficiency 38.7 %
Compare the raw cell efficiency 48 / 53 = 90.6 %: the trailer and padding cost extra
PPP in more detail:
items: Byte stuffing (RFC 1662): a data byte 0x7E is sent as 0x7D 0x5E and a byte 0x7D as 0x7D 0x5D (the escape byte, then the original byte XOR 0x20); control characters below 0x20 are escaped too unless LCP negotiates this away with the ACCM option.
LCP options include the MRU (default 1500 bytes), the authentication protocol, a magic number that detects looped-back links, and compression of the address/control and protocol fields.
IPCP, the NCP for IPv4, lets the ISP assign the client's IP address and DNS servers; IPV6CP only negotiates a 64-bit interface identifier, and the IPv6 address itself then comes from SLAAC or DHCPv6.

PPPoE (RFC 2516) carries PPP over Ethernet for DSL: a discovery stage (PADI, PADO, PADR, PADS) finds the access concentrator and a session ID, and the 6-byte PPPoE header plus the 2-byte PPP protocol field cut the MTU from 1500 to 1492 bytes.
Multilink PPP bundles several physical links into one logical link and spreads fragments across them.

concepts.text:
Worked trace: CHAP authentication (RFC 1994) after LCP has agreed on CHAP with MD5
Authenticator -> peer: Challenge (identifier 7, random challenge value C)
Peer -> authenticator: Response  (identifier 7, MD5(7 || shared secret || C), name)
Authenticator computes the same hash from its own copy of the secret and compares
Authenticator -> peer: Success (or Failure, and the link is terminated)
Repeated at random intervals with a new challenge, so an old response cannot be replayed
PAP for comparison: peer -> authenticator: user name + password in clear text; ACK or NAK

HDLC is the parent of a family of WAN link protocols: LAPB for X.25, LAPD for the ISDN D channel, LAPF for Frame Relay and the HDLC-like framing of PPP. Frame Relay traffic contracts use the committed information rate (CIR), the committed burst Bc = CIR × Tc allowed in each measurement interval Tc, and an excess burst Be: data up to Bc is forwarded normally, data between Bc and Bc + Be is forwarded but marked discard eligible (DE = 1) so that a congested switch drops it first, and anything beyond Bc + Be is discarded at once, while the FECN and BECN bits warn the end systems of congestion. X.25 works in three layers (X.21 physical, LAPB link and the packet layer protocol) and checks errors at every hop, which is exactly the work Frame Relay removed. An MPLS shim header is 32 bits: a 20-bit label, 3 traffic-class bits, a bottom-of-stack bit S and an 8-bit TTL, and label switch routers push, swap or pop labels as packets cross the network.

Common mistakes: ARP requests are broadcast but replies are unicast; ARP works only within one link, so a host never ARPs for a remote destination, only for its gateway; RARP (MAC to IP) is obsolete and replaced by DHCP; the ATM header is 5 bytes and the payload 48, not the other way round; a Frame Relay DLCI has only local significance, so the two ends of one virtual circuit may use different numbers; and PAP sends the password in clear text.

notes.text: ARP request = broadcast, ARP reply = unicast. RARP goes the other way (MAC to IP). For PPP, remember LCP sets up the link, NCP (IPCP) sets up the network protocol, and CHAP is safer than PAP.
A MAC address is only meaningful on the local link: routers rewrite source and destination MAC addresses at every hop, while the IP addresses stay the same end to end (without NAT).
The ATM cell size of 53 bytes was a compromise between 32 and 64 bytes of payload proposed by different countries; the small cell keeps voice packetisation delay low.

formulas.title: MAC address space
formulas.description: A 48-bit MAC splits into a 24-bit vendor OUI and a 24-bit interface-specific part.

formulas.title: ATM cell efficiency
formulas.description: Fraction of each 53-byte ATM cell that carries user payload; the 5-byte header is overhead.

formulas.title: PPP frame overhead
formulas.plainText: flag + address + control + protocol + FCS(2) + flag = 8 bytes
formulas.description: Bytes PPP adds around each payload with a 16-bit FCS and separate opening and closing flags.

flashcards.front: Why is an ARP request broadcast but the reply unicast?
flashcards.back: The sender does not yet know the target's MAC, so it must ask everyone; the owner knows the requester's MAC from the request and answers it directly.

flashcards.front: What do LCP and NCP do in PPP?
flashcards.back: LCP establishes, configures and tests the link; each NCP (such as IPCP) configures a network-layer protocol over it.

flashcards.front: What are DLCI and CIR in Frame Relay?
flashcards.back: DLCI is the 10-bit virtual-circuit identifier in each frame; CIR is the committed information rate the carrier guarantees for that circuit.

flashcards.front: What is proxy ARP?
flashcards.back: A router replies to ARP requests for hosts on another network with its own MAC, then forwards the traffic to them.

questions.questionText: What is the total size of an ATM cell?
questions.explanation: An ATM cell is fixed at 53 bytes: a 5-byte header and a 48-byte payload.

questions.questionText: Why is CHAP considered more secure than PAP for PPP authentication?
options: CHAP encrypts all user data on the link
CHAP never sends the password; it answers a random challenge with a hash
CHAP uses a longer clear-text password
CHAP runs before LCP link establishment
questions.explanation: CHAP's three-way handshake sends only an MD5 hash of the challenge and shared secret, and changing challenges defeat replay; PAP sends the password in clear text.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of a MAC address?
options: To identify a network interface on the local link, so that frames reach the right device
To identify the IP version in use
To identify a host end to end across the Internet
To encrypt the frames sent on the link
questions.explanation: A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware address used for delivery within one LAN or link, and routers replace the MAC header at every hop. End-to-end identification across networks is the job of the IP address.

questions.questionText: What does ARP stand for?
questions.explanation: ARP is the Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826), which finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on the local network. Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) is an error-control method, not ARP.

questions.questionText: RARP (Reverse ARP) was used by a host to find:
options: A MAC address from a known IP address
An IP address from a domain name
Its IP address from its known MAC address
An IP address from a port number
questions.explanation: RARP let a diskless machine that knew only its MAC address ask a server for its IP address at boot. It is obsolete: BOOTP and then DHCP replaced it, because they also supply the subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers and can be relayed across routers.

questions.questionText: What does a host's ARP table (ARP cache) store?
options: The IP addresses of DNS servers
Recently resolved IP-to-MAC address mappings, each with a timeout
questions.explanation: The ARP cache keeps IP-to-MAC mappings learned from ARP replies (and requests) so that later packets need no new broadcast; entries age out after a timeout, typically a few minutes. Routes are kept in the routing table.

questions.questionText: A frame has the destination MAC address 3A:9C:10:00:4E:21. What kind of address is it?
questions.explanation: The first byte 0x3A = 0011 1010. Its least significant bit (I/G) is 0, so the address is unicast, and the next bit (U/L) is 1, so it is locally administered rather than built on an IEEE OUI.

questions.questionText: A MAC address has a 24-bit OUI followed by 24 bits assigned by the manufacturer. How many distinct addresses can a manufacturer assign under one OUI?
questions.explanation: The 24 vendor bits give 2^24 = 16,777,216 combinations, and none is reserved in the way IP subnets reserve network and broadcast addresses. 2^48 is the size of the whole MAC address space.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 multicast datagram for group 239.129.1.5 is sent on an Ethernet LAN. Which destination MAC address does the frame use?
questions.explanation: The MAC is 01:00:5E followed by a 0 bit and the low 23 bits of the group address. 129 = 1000 0001, and dropping its top bit leaves 000 0001, so the last three bytes are 01:01:05, giving 01:00:5E:01:01:05; 01:00:5E:81:01:05 wrongly copies all 24 bits.

questions.questionText: Which statement about ARP messages on an Ethernet LAN is correct?
options: Both the ARP request and the ARP reply are broadcast
The ARP request is unicast to the router and the reply is broadcast
The ARP request is broadcast to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF and the reply is unicast to the requester
ARP messages travel inside IP datagrams with protocol number 0x0806
questions.explanation: The requester does not yet know the target's MAC address, so the request must be broadcast; the target knows the requester's MAC from the request and replies to it directly. ARP is carried straight in Ethernet frames with EtherType 0x0806, not inside IP.

questions.questionText: Which EtherType value identifies an ARP message inside an Ethernet frame?
questions.explanation: ARP uses EtherType 0x0806. 0x0800 is IPv4, 0x86DD is IPv6 and 0x8035 was used by RARP.

questions.questionText: Host A (192.168.1.10/24, default gateway 192.168.1.1) sends its first packet to 8.8.8.8 with an empty ARP cache. Which IP address does its ARP request ask about?
questions.explanation: 8.8.8.8 is outside 192.168.1.0/24, so A must hand the packet to its default gateway and needs the gateway's MAC address; it therefore ARPs for 192.168.1.1. ARP never resolves addresses beyond the local link.

questions.questionText: Host A (10.0.0.5/24) sends an IP packet to host B (10.0.1.7/24) through router R, whose interface on A's network is 10.0.0.1. Which destination addresses does the frame leaving A carry?
options: Destination MAC = B's MAC, destination IP = 10.0.1.7
Destination MAC = R's MAC, destination IP = 10.0.0.1
Destination MAC = R's MAC, destination IP = 10.0.1.7
questions.explanation: A sees that 10.0.1.7 is not in 10.0.0.0/24, so it sends the frame to the next hop: R's MAC address, learned by ARP for 10.0.0.1. The IP header keeps the final destination 10.0.1.7, and R builds a new frame towards B.

questions.questionText: Right after its interface comes up, a host sends an ARP request asking for its own IP address. What is this gratuitous ARP mainly used for?
options: Detecting another host that already uses the same IP address and updating other hosts' ARP caches
Obtaining an IP address from a server
Finding the MAC address of the default gateway
Measuring the round-trip time to the switch
questions.explanation: If any host answers a gratuitous ARP, the address is already in use; if not, the announcement refreshes the mapping in other hosts' caches, which is also how a standby router or server takes over an address after failover.

questions.questionText: A router answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts on another network, replying with its own MAC address so that traffic for them is sent to the router. This is called:
questions.explanation: In proxy ARP (RFC 1027) the router answers for the remote hosts and then forwards the frames it receives. Inverse ARP finds the IP address at the far end of a Frame Relay DLCI, and reverse ARP maps a MAC address to an IP address.

questions.questionText: Why is ARP spoofing (ARP cache poisoning) possible, and what counters it on a switched LAN?
options: ARP replies are not authenticated, so hosts accept forged mappings; dynamic ARP inspection on switches checks them against trusted bindings
ARP runs over TCP, whose sequence numbers can be guessed; SYN cookies counter it
ARP requests are unicast, so they can be intercepted; broadcasting them counters it
ARP entries never expire; rebooting the router counters it
questions.explanation: Hosts accept unsolicited or forged ARP replies because ARP has no authentication, so an attacker can map the gateway's IP to its own MAC and sit in the middle. Dynamic ARP inspection drops ARP packets that do not match the DHCP-snooping bindings; static entries also help on small networks.

questions.questionText: An ARP message for IPv4 over Ethernet is 28 bytes long. How many pad bytes does the Ethernet frame carrying it need?
questions.explanation: The ARP message is 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 28 bytes, but the Ethernet data field must be at least 46 bytes, so 46 − 28 = 18 pad bytes are added and the frame is 14 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes. 36 wrongly pads up to 64 bytes of data.

questions.questionText: In PPP, which protocol establishes, configures and tests the data link before any network-layer traffic flows?
questions.explanation: The Link Control Protocol negotiates options such as the MRU, authentication method and magic number, and tests the link. NCPs such as IPCP run only afterwards to configure each network-layer protocol, and CHAP is an authentication protocol.

questions.questionText: A home router connects to its ISP over PPPoE and receives its public IPv4 address during PPP setup. Which protocol assigns it?
questions.explanation: After LCP and authentication, the IP Control Protocol (an NCP) negotiates the IPv4 address and can also supply DNS server addresses. LCP configures only the link and PAP only authenticates.

questions.questionText: What is the correct order of PPP phases for a link that uses authentication?
options: Dead, Establish (LCP), Authenticate, Network (NCP), Open, Terminate
Dead, Authenticate, Establish (LCP), Network (NCP), Open, Terminate
Dead, Network (NCP), Establish (LCP), Open, Authenticate, Terminate
questions.explanation: The link starts dead, LCP establishes it, the optional authentication (PAP or CHAP) follows, NCPs such as IPCP configure the network layer, data flows in the open state and LCP finally terminates the link. Authentication cannot come before LCP, because LCP negotiates which method to use.

questions.questionText: Why is the Address field of a PPP frame always 0xFF?
options: It carries the destination IP address in compressed form
A point-to-point link has only one possible receiver, so the all-stations address is used and no real addressing is needed
It marks the start of the frame
It shows that the frame contains an LCP message
questions.explanation: PPP keeps the HDLC frame layout but, with only two ends on the link, fixes the address at 0xFF (all stations) and the control field at 0x03; LCP can even negotiate leaving both out. The start of a frame is marked by the flag 0x7E, and the Protocol field identifies LCP (0xC021).

questions.questionText: PPP with HDLC-like framing (RFC 1662) must send the payload bytes 7E 41 7D 42. Assuming only the flag and escape bytes need escaping, which bytes are transmitted between the flags?
questions.explanation: Each 0x7E or 0x7D in the data is replaced by the escape byte 0x7D followed by the original byte XOR 0x20: 7E becomes 7D 5E and 7D becomes 7D 5D, while 41 and 42 pass unchanged. Putting 7D in front of an unchanged byte is the simplified textbook form of byte stuffing, not the exact PPP rule.

questions.questionText: Why is the MTU on a PPPoE DSL link usually 1492 bytes rather than 1500?
options: The 6-byte PPPoE header and the 2-byte PPP protocol field use 8 bytes of the 1500-byte Ethernet payload
The 8-byte preamble must fit inside the Ethernet payload
PPP adds a 4-byte FCS and 4 bytes of flags inside the payload
DSL lines cannot carry frames longer than 1492 bytes
questions.explanation: PPPoE puts a 6-byte header and the 2-byte PPP protocol ID inside the Ethernet data field, leaving 1500 − 8 = 1492 bytes for the IP packet. PPPoE frames carry no PPP flags or FCS because Ethernet's own CRC protects them.

questions.questionText: In PPP CHAP (RFC 1994) with MD5, how does the peer compute its Response value?
options: As the MD5 hash of the password alone
As the MD5 hash of the identifier, the shared secret and the challenge, concatenated
By encrypting the password with DES, using the challenge as the key
By returning the challenge unchanged together with the user name
questions.explanation: The response is MD5(identifier ‖ secret ‖ challenge); the authenticator computes the same value from its own copy of the secret. A hash of the password alone would be the same every time and could simply be replayed.

questions.questionText: Which HDLC-based protocol is the data link layer of X.25?
questions.explanation: X.25 uses LAPB (Link Access Procedure, Balanced) between the DTE and the network. LAPD serves the ISDN D channel, LAPF serves Frame Relay, and PPP uses HDLC-like framing for point-to-point links.

questions.questionText: In Frame Relay, what identifies a virtual circuit on a link?
questions.explanation: Frame Relay marks each frame with a DLCI, normally 10 bits long and significant only on the local link. VPI/VCI belongs to ATM, the 20-bit label to MPLS and the logical channel number to X.25.

questions.questionText: A Frame Relay circuit has CIR = 64 kbps, measurement interval Tc = 1 s and excess burst Be = 32 kbits. In one interval the user sends 120 kbits. How much of this data is forwarded but marked discard eligible (DE = 1)?
questions.explanation: Bc = CIR × Tc = 64 kbits is forwarded normally; the next Be = 32 kbits (up to Bc + Be = 96 kbits) is forwarded with DE = 1; the remaining 120 − 96 = 24 kbits are discarded. 56 kbits would mark all the excess as DE.

questions.questionText: A 1500-byte IP packet is carried over ATM using AAL5, which adds an 8-byte trailer and pads to a multiple of 48 bytes. How many cells are needed, and what is the efficiency (IP bytes divided by bytes on the line)?
questions.explanation: (1500 + 8) / 48 = 31.4, so 32 cells are needed, occupying 32 × 53 = 1696 bytes, and the efficiency is 1500 / 1696 = 88.4%. 90.6% is only the raw 48/53 cell efficiency, and 29 cells wrongly divides by 53 instead of 48.

questions.questionText: Why does ATM use small, fixed-size 53-byte cells?
options: To keep queuing and packetisation delay low and predictable for voice and video, and to allow fast hardware switching
To reduce header overhead compared with large frames
To avoid the need for virtual circuits
So that each cell fits in an Ethernet minimum frame
questions.explanation: Short fixed cells mean a voice cell never waits long behind a large data packet, and fixed sizes make switching simple enough for hardware. The price is a relatively high header overhead (5 of every 53 bytes), and ATM is built on virtual circuits (VPI/VCI).

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing X.25 and Frame Relay is correct?
options: Frame Relay performs error control and retransmission at every switch, unlike X.25
X.25 checks and corrects errors at every hop, while Frame Relay only discards bad frames and leaves recovery to the end systems
Both carry data in fixed 53-byte cells
X.25 is connectionless, while Frame Relay is connection-oriented
questions.explanation: X.25 was designed for noisy analogue lines and does error and flow control hop by hop; Frame Relay assumes clean digital links, checks the FCS and silently drops bad frames, leaving retransmission to protocols such as TCP. Both are connection-oriented, using virtual circuits.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the MPLS shim header is correct?
options: It sits between the layer 2 header and the IP header and carries a 20-bit label, 3 traffic-class bits, a bottom-of-stack bit and an 8-bit TTL
It replaces the IP header and carries 32-bit source and destination labels
It is placed after the TCP header and carries a 16-bit label
It is a 5-byte header with VPI and VCI fields
questions.explanation: The 32-bit MPLS header (20 + 3 + 1 + 8 bits) is inserted between layers 2 and 3, which is why MPLS is called layer 2.5, and several headers can be stacked. VPI and VCI belong to the 5-byte ATM cell header.

questions.questionText: A packet travels from host A across two routers to host B, with no NAT on the path. Which addresses are rewritten at every router hop?
options: The source and destination IP addresses
The source and destination MAC addresses
questions.explanation: Each router removes the incoming frame and builds a new one with its own outgoing MAC as source and the next hop's MAC as destination. The IP addresses stay the same end to end (only the TTL and header checksum change).
